  Learn how to download processed files, raw sequencing reads, and alignment BAMs
  for genomic accessions, verify checksums, and manage data storage.

  rmarkdown::html_document:

```{r, include = FALSE}
seqout::SeqoutDefault(NULL)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Three functions download files to disk:

*   `DownloadSupplementary()`: processed supplementary files (counts matrices, annotations, archives).
*   `DownloadRuns()`: raw reads.
*   `DownloadBAMs()`: submitted alignment files (BAMs).

You must give `dest_dir` to each function. The function writes the files into that directory. If the directory does not exist, the function makes it. The examples in this article use the accession as the directory name. The three functions verify checksums and skip the files that are already on disk.

```{r setup}
library(seqout)
```

## Examine the files before you download them

A dataset can have a size of tens of gigabytes. Thus, examine the files first. The `supplementary` field of `SeqoutGet()` lists the processed supplementary files. `SeqoutGet()` does not download these files:

```{r listing}
d <- SeqoutGet("GSE168652")

head(d$supplementary, 4)
```

A file that is directly related to the series has `NA` in the `sample` column. Each other file is related to one sample.

For GEO, ArrayExpress and DDBJ GEA projects, `SupplementaryFiles()` lists the same files. For each file, the result also gives a download command and the result of the seqout scan for gene names that Excel damaged. For example, Excel changes `"SEPT1"` to `"1-Sep"`. If `gene_corruption` is `NULL`, seqout did not scan the file, and the file can contain gene names that Excel damaged:

```{r supp-files}
sf <- SupplementaryFiles("GSE168652")
sf[, c("filename", "download_command")]
```

The `runs` field lists the raw reads. It has one URL column for each archive mirror:

```{r runs-listing}
runs <- SeqoutGet("SRP150719")$runs

nrow(runs)
head(runs[, c("run_accession", "library_layout", "fastq_bytes", "fastq_ftp")], 3)
```

For a paired-end run, one cell holds the two read files with a semicolon between them. The checksum cells use the same format.

`RunFiles()` divides those cells into one row for each file, with the size and the checksum of the file. It selects the same copy that `DownloadRuns()` will download. Thus, you can calculate the total size of a download before you start it:

```{r run-files}
files <- RunFiles(runs, mode = "fastq")
head(files, 4)
sprintf("%d files, %.1f GB", nrow(files), sum(files$bytes, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9)
```

## Download processed files

`DownloadSupplementary()` downloads the processed files that the authors uploaded:

```{r supp, eval = FALSE}
DownloadSupplementary("GSE168652", "GSE168652")
```

The type of accession sets the scope:

| Accession Type | Download Scope |
| --- | --- |
| Series or Study (e.g., GSE, SRP) | The study and all its samples. |
| GEO Sample (GSM) | That sample only. |
| Experiment, Run, or BioSample | An error. These accessions host no processed files. |

The error message asks for the accession of the parent project. Thus, a full study does not go into a directory that has the name of one sample or one run.

```{r supp-error, error = TRUE}
DownloadSupplementary("SRR12012336", "SRR12012336")
```

SRA, ENA, DDBJ, and GSA do not hold processed supplementary files. The linked GEO or ArrayExpress records hold these files. `DownloadSupplementary()` follows the link and downloads them.

```{r supp-ae, eval = FALSE}
DownloadSupplementary("E-MTAB-11467", "E-MTAB-11467") # Downloads processed archives and raw files
```

## Download raw reads

`DownloadRuns()` downloads raw reads. The accession sets the scope:

*   For a run accession (SRR), the function downloads only that run.
*   For an experiment (SRX) or sample (SRS) accession, the function downloads all the runs linked to it.
*   For a study or series accession (SRP/GSE), the function downloads all the runs of the full study.

```{r runs, eval = FALSE}
DownloadRuns("SRR12012336", "SRR12012336")
```

### Choose a download mode

The archives supply reads in different formats. The `mode` argument selects one format:

| Mode | Format Details |
| --- | --- |
| `"fastq"` | FASTQ files hosted by ENA, verified against published MD5 checksums. |
| `"sra"` | NCBI's SRA format with full-quality data. |
| `"sra_lite"` | NCBI's SRA format with binned quality scores. |

If you do not set `mode`, the function downloads the first available format in the order of the table. It also gives an R warning. Always set `mode`:

```{r runs-mode, eval = FALSE}
DownloadRuns("SRP150719", "SRP150719", mode = "fastq")
```

> [!WARNING]
> Binned quality scores have less detail. Use `"sra_lite"` only if smaller files are more important to you than that detail.

For a study accession, the function shows the number of runs and the estimated size before the download starts:

```{r runs-study, eval = FALSE}
DownloadRuns("SRP267291", "SRP267291") # Downloads 34 runs
```

Some runs are only in requester-pays cloud buckets (AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage). These buckets send the bill to the caller. The function refuses `mode = "s3"` and `mode = "gcs"` for anonymous access and stops with an error. If a mirror that all users can read exists, the error message gives that mirror.

### File names and integrity

FASTQ downloads keep the file names from ENA, for example the `_1` and `_2` suffixes of paired-end runs. Downstream tools expect these names.

NCBI supplies SRA files without extensions. `DownloadRuns` adds an extension, for example `SRR12012336.sra`, or `SRR12012336_1.sra` for multi-file runs.

If the archive publishes a checksum, the function verifies the file before it moves the file to its final destination. All ENA FASTQ files have a checksum. If the verification fails, the function deletes the file.

Each download writes to a temporary `.part` file. Thus, an interrupted download cannot overwrite a complete file.

## Download alignment files

`DownloadBAMs()` downloads the BAM files that the authors uploaded. These files hold the alignments that the authors made against their selected reference. The files frequently keep metadata that the raw reads do not have. Examples are barcode tags, methylation marks, and structural variant details.

The `bams` field lists the files before you download them:

```{r bams-listing}
b <- SeqoutGet("ERP117016")$bams

nrow(b)
head(b[, c("filename", "size", "md5")], 3)
```

```{r bams, eval = FALSE}
DownloadBAMs("ERP117016", "ERP117016")
```

Many alignment files are in requester-pays cloud storage. `DownloadBAMs()` cannot download these files with anonymous access. For these files, it lists the filenames. It also prints the `aws` commands that download the files with your own credentials:

```{r bams-paid}
paid <- SeqoutGet("SRP071083")$bams

nrow(paid)
head(paid[, c("filename", "size", "s3_url")], 3)
```

## Download the database dump

The Parquet backend reads the published dump remotely. For work that is fully offline, `DownloadDump()` downloads the tables to disk. It shows the total size first. `Tables()` gives the names of the tables that you can request:

```{r dump, eval = FALSE}
DownloadDump(dest_dir = "~/seqout-dump", tables = c("unified_metadata", "geo_series"))

con <- SeqoutConnect("parquet", data_dir = "~/seqout-dump")
Query("SELECT count(*) FROM unified_metadata", con = con)
```

## Archive file support matrix

| Archive | Processed Files | Raw Reads | Submitted Alignments |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| GEO | Yes (Series and Samples) | Via linked SRA study | Rare |
| ArrayExpress & GEA | Yes (Processed and Raw) | Via linked ENA study | Rare |
| SRA, ENA, DDBJ | No | Yes | Sometimes |
| GSA | No | Yes | Sometimes |

`SeqoutGet()` resolves the cross-references between these archives. Thus, one accession gives access to all the related files.
